title: The family
heading: One shape, many relatives
intro: Over-robe, jacket, trousers, under-robe: one family. Each member signals the occasion and season, and the wearer's age and standing {4:p.11}.

label.title: Long-Sleeved Robe (Furisode) with Phoenixes, Cherry Blossoms, Peonies, and Maple Branches
label.material: Crepe silk with silk and gold-thread embroidery
label.insight: In the Edo period worn mainly by children of affluent families {4:p.53}. Today <q>mainly reserved for unmarried women to wear at formal occasions</q> {4:p.53}.

label.title: Over Robe (Uchikake) with Fans and Flowers
label.meta: Japan · Edo period · second half 18th–first half 19th century
label.material: Figured satin-weave silk with tie-dyeing, silk embroidery, and couched gold thread
label.insight: Uchikake became bridal wear: white, over kosode, in the Muromachi warrior class {38:p.42}; since the war, in colour for the wedding reception {38:p.43}.

label.title: Kosode
label.material: Crests, perhaps bamboo, reserved in white.
label.insight: A Kyoto dealer's manual of the 1760s tags dyed cloth by whether family crests were put on it {13:p.71}. By 1968 one town kept crests mainly for ceremonial dress {32:p.63}.

label.title: Man's Formal Jacket (Haori)
label.insight: First men's dress, layered over the kosode {37:P-386}. Under the clothing laws, merchants hid colour and embroidery on the inner layer of the haori {4:pp.99-100}.

label.title: Man's Trousers (Hakama)
label.insight: Edo period, with a haori: everyday wear for samurai, formal wear for townsmen {37:P-386}. Kyoto, 2018: about 30% of men at the coming-of-age day, Becke estimates {4:p.104}.

label.title: Inner garment (nagajuban)
label.insight: The first layer on, in magazine dressing columns {4:p.72}. It changes with the season too: silk or polyester October to May, ro or sha June to September {6:p.20}.

label.title: Fireman’s Jacket (Hikeshi-Banten) with Susanoo-no-mikoto Deity Scene
label.meta: Japanese · Edo or Meiji period · mid-19th century
label.material: Quilted cotton with tube-drawn paste-resist dyeing (tsutsugaki) with hand-painted details
label.insight: Cotton, not silk. Early Edo clothing laws marked rank by the cloth itself: silk for those above, then pongee, cotton and hemp {39:p.438}.

cards.title: Ranked, top to bottom
body: The usual order, as a 2022 study of the kimono trade states it {25:p.16}. Tsumugi, between komon and yukata there, is left out: no source here defines it.
head: What sets it apart
rows: About the same rank as hōmongi {33:p.422}
One colour, no pattern; suits tea {25:p.16}

cards.title: The same ladder, for men
body: By the mid-Edo period a black crested haori was the most formal; plain, then komon, then stripes were each less formal {37:P-386}.
When the Meiji Restoration abolished the kamishimo, haori and hakama became men's formal dress, as they still are {37:P-386}.

cues.show: Begin with the long sleeves. In the late Edo period, the writer Kitagawa Morisada sorted the robes of his day into four grades, from formal down to everyday. For a woman's formal dress, the older the wearer, the quieter the pattern.
cues.say: Begin with the long sleeves. In the late Edo period, the writer Kee-tah-gah-wah Moh-ree-sah-dah sorted the robes of his day into four grades, from formal down to everyday. For a woman's formal dress, the older the wearer, the quieter the pattern.

cues.show: Today the long-sleeved robe is the kimono a Japanese woman is most likely ever to buy.
Sleeves could also be cut down. In wartime, brides wore a black furisode with a train, because its sleeves could later be shortened to make a tomesode, a married woman's formal robe.
A survey in one Tottori town, in the late nineteen-sixties, counted two hundred and six different crests.
cues.say: A survey in one Toh-toh-ree town, in the late nineteen-sixties, counted two hundred and six different crests.

cues.show: The jacket is the easiest member to borrow. In Kyoto's flea markets, visitors take to the haori because it needs no obi and no wrapping.
Rules reached even the plainest cloth. Edo law told peasants to wear plain dark blue, and the order went out across the whole country.
Each rule had its date. The next stretch of wall walks through them.

claims.text: Kimono design signals the formality of the event and the season.
claims.quote: the level of the perceived formality of the event the garment is worn to, as well as the seasonal context
claims.scope: Becke, citing Dalby 2001: 164; general

claims.text: Design also signals the wearer's gender, age, standing and taste.
claims.quote: personal attributes such as the wearer’s gender, age, social standing and taste
claims.scope: Becke, citing Dalby 2001: 164; general

claims.text: In the Edo period the furisode was mainly worn by children of affluent families.
claims.quote: the garment mainly being worn by children of affluent families during the Edo period
claims.scope: Becke, citing Sawada 2006; Edo period

claims.text: The furisode is mainly reserved for unmarried women at formal occasions.
claims.quote: mainly reserved for unmarried women to wear at formal occasions
claims.scope: Becke, citing Dalby 2001: 172, Goldstein-Gidoni 1999, Milhaupt 2014: 38; present day

claims.text: In the Muromachi period bridal dress became fixed as a white uchikake over kosode.
claims.quote: 婚礼衣裳も白打掛に小袖と定まった (Tr. "bridal dress too became fixed as a white uchikake over kosode")
claims.scope: Dōmae 2015, college bulletin, not refereed; summary of secondary literature; warrior class

claims.text: After the war, shiromuku for the Shinto rite and a coloured uchikake for the reception became usual.
claims.quote: 神前結婚式では白無垢、披露宴で色打掛が主流となった (Tr. "white shiromuku became mainstream for Shinto weddings and coloured uchikake for receptions")
claims.scope: Dōmae 2015, college bulletin, not refereed; post-war

claims.text: In wartime the black trailing furisode became the main bridal dress because its sleeves could be shortened to make a tomesode.
claims.quote: 袖を詰めて留袖として生かせる黒引き振袖が主流となった (Tr. "the black trailing furisode, which could be reused as a tomesode by shortening the sleeves, became mainstream")
claims.scope: Dōmae 2015, college bulletin, not refereed; Shōwa wartime

claims.text: In 18th-century Kyoto, dyed fabrics were tagged by whether family crests were put on them.
claims.quote: distinguished by tags attached, on the basis of whether or not family crests are put on them
claims.scope: Suzuki 2022, on the Daikokuya manual, Kyoto, 1768-69; crests dyed in before sale

claims.text: By the late 1960s crests on clothing were seldom seen except on ceremonial dress.
claims.quote: 被服に紋章をとり入れる傾向は、式服を除いてはあまりみられなくなった (Tr. "the tendency to put crests on clothing is seldom seen now, except on ceremonial dress")
claims.scope: Fukui 1970, refereed short report; one town (Kurayoshi, Tottori), 1967-68

claims.text: One town's survey found 206 kinds of crest.
claims.quote: 紋章の種類は206種類である (Tr. "there are 206 kinds of crest")
claims.scope: Fukui 1970, refereed short report; Kurayoshi, Tottori, questionnaire 1967-68

claims.text: The haori was originally men's dress, layered over the kosode.
claims.quote: 元来、羽織は男装であり、小袖の上に表衣として着重ねられる着衣である (Tr. "originally the haori was men's dress, a garment layered over the kosode as the outer robe")
claims.scope: Yokogawa 2008, invited essay, not refereed

claims.text: Under sumptuary law, merchants hid colour and embroidery inside their haori.
claims.quote: colourful patterns and intricate embroidery were added to the inner layer of haori jackets to hide them from view
claims.scope: Edo; Becke, citing Motoji and Motoji 2017: 36-37

claims.text: In the Edo period haori with hakama became samurai everyday dress and townsmen's formal dress.
claims.quote: 羽織袴姿として様式化を遂げ、武士の日常着、町人の礼服となる (Tr. "became standardised as haori-hakama dress: everyday wear for samurai, formal wear for townsmen")
claims.scope: Yokogawa 2008, invited essay, not refereed; Edo period

claims.text: Becke estimates about 30% of men wore hakama and haori at Kyoto's coming-of-age ceremony in 2018.
claims.quote: I would estimate that roughly thirty percent of male attendees dressed in hakama and haori for the coming-of-age ceremony in Kyoto in 2018
claims.scope: Becke's own very limited observation; Kyoto only

claims.text: Magazine dressing columns run from putting on the nagajuban to tying the obi knot.
claims.quote: from putting on the nagajuban (under-kimono) to the final tying of the obi knot
claims.scope: furisode; magazine kitsuke columns

claims.text: The nagajuban also changes by season.
claims.quote: warm materials such as silk or polyester used from October to May, thinner fabrics such as ro or sha from June to September
claims.scope: Druet 2024; general, present day

claims.text: In the early shogunate rank was shown by material: silk above, then pongee, cotton and hemp.
claims.quote: 幕政初期には上位の者に絹,続いて紬,木綿,布と衣服材料でもって身分差を示そうとした (Tr. "in the early shogunate they tried to show rank by material: silk for those above, then tsumugi, cotton and hemp cloth")
claims.scope: Nishimura 1980, refereed; summary of 250 years of edicts. The jacket is not claimed to follow any law.

claims.text: Peasants' clothing was to be plain dark blue, a rule proclaimed across the country.
claims.quote: 百姓の衣類は紺無地とする規制が全国に触れ渡っている (Tr. "the rule that peasants' clothes be plain dark blue was proclaimed throughout the country")
claims.scope: Nishimura 1980, refereed; Edo period

claims.text: Usual ranking: furisode first formal wear, black tomesode for married women, then hōmongi, tsukesage, iromuji, komon, tsumugi, yukata.
claims.quote: 第一礼装は振袖，既婚女性は黒留袖，訪問着，付下げ，色無地，小紋，紬，浴衣とランクづけされている (Tr. "ranked: first formal wear furisode, for married women black tomesode, homongi, tsukesage, iromuji, komon, tsumugi, yukata")
claims.scope: Araki 2022, business-studies paper stating a general convention; not a costume-history source

claims.text: Iromuji is white silk dyed one colour, without pattern, suiting the restraint of tea.
claims.quote: 色無地は，白生地を一色に染めたもので，柄がなく派手すぎないため，華美を避ける茶道の精神に通じる (Tr. "iromuji is white cloth dyed in one colour; with no pattern and not too showy, it suits the spirit of tea, which avoids display")
claims.scope: Araki 2022, business-studies paper

claims.text: Hōmongi are worn at weddings, parties and tea gatherings.
claims.quote: 結婚式やパーティー，お茶会等，幅広い場面で着用されている (Tr. "worn on a wide range of occasions such as weddings, parties and tea gatherings")
claims.scope: Furukawa 2021, refereed; present day

claims.text: Hōmongi and tsukesage are almost the same in formality.
claims.quote: 訪問着と付け下げは格式としてはほぼ同じでパーティーやお茶会などで着られる (Tr. "hōmongi and tsukesage are almost the same in formality and are worn at parties, tea gatherings and so on")
claims.scope: Okamoto, Numata, Kōyama 2008, magazine review, not refereed; norm c.2005

claims.text: The furisode is the Japanese garment a woman today is most likely to buy in her lifetime.
claims.quote: 振袖は近年の女性が生涯で購入する可能性の一番高い和服であり，成人式との関係が深い (Tr. "the furisode is the Japanese garment a woman today is most likely to buy in her lifetime, and is closely tied to the coming-of-age ceremony")
claims.scope: Okamoto, Numata, Kōyama 2008, not refereed; authors' statement

claims.text: Komon: small patterns repeated all over the garment.
claims.quote: Komon designates a kimono with small patterns duplicated all over the surface of the garment.
claims.scope: Druet 2021, note 38

claims.text: The yukata is an unlined kimono of light cotton.
claims.quote: yukata (浴衣 unlined kimono made of light cotton)
claims.scope: Druet 2024; general

claims.text: In mid-Edo the black crested haori became most formal; plain, komon and stripes were progressively less formal.
claims.quote: 江戸中期には黒紋付（羽二重・縮緬など）が最も正式なものとなる。と同時に無地・小紋・縞の順に略式とされ (Tr. "in mid-Edo the black crested [haori] became the most formal; plain, komon and stripes were, in that order, less formal")
claims.scope: Yokogawa 2008, invited essay, not refereed; men's haori

claims.text: Since the kamishimo was abolished after the Meiji Restoration, haori and hakama have been men's formal dress.
claims.quote: 明治維新以後に裃が廃止されてから今日に至るまで、男子の礼装として広く用いられている (Tr. "since the kamishimo was abolished after the Meiji Restoration, it has been widely used as men's formal dress to this day")
claims.scope: Yokogawa 2008, invited essay, not refereed

claims.text: Kitagawa Morisada sorted the kosode of his day into four grades: formal, best, informal, everyday.
claims.quote: 当時の小袖の種類を「礼」「晴」「略」「褻」の４つに区分している (Tr. "divides the kosode of the time into four kinds: rei, hare, ryaku and ke")
claims.scope: Furukawa 2021, refereed, reading Morisada mankō (mid-19th century)

claims.text: In late-Edo women's formal dress, the older the wearer, the more restrained the pattern.
claims.quote: 模様は年齢に応じて，その有無や表し方が決まっており，年齢が高くなれば模様は控えめに (Tr. "whether there was a pattern, and how it was shown, was set by age; the older the wearer, the more restrained the pattern")
claims.scope: Furukawa 2021, refereed; late Edo, from Morisada mankō

claims.text: In Kyoto flea markets the haori is popular because it needs no obi or wrapping.
claims.quote: A haori doesn’t require an obi or any kind of wrapping, folding components to be worn properly.
claims.scope: Druet 2021; Kyoto flea markets, 2018-21

dropped: Noh costume 45190: the only source line is that Nishijin weavers traditionally made Nō costumes (12 p.65); nothing compares Nō dress with the kimono, and the wall is kept to seven photographs.
Crest counts by formality (one, three, five crests): only Meiji visiting wear (three embroidered crests, 29 p.19) and late-Edo bridal furisode (five crests, 38 p.43) are sourced; no general rule.
Sleeve lengths in centimetres for furisode and tomesode, and the tomesode's hem-only pattern as a present-day rule: not in the sources read.
What the fireman's jacket was for (soaking, firefighting): no source read.
Tsumugi as a fabric: ranked (25 p.16) but not defined anywhere, so left out of the table.
